newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Business as unusual for Body Shop founder.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Business as unusual for Body Shop founder.

text.p: Maverick entrepreneur Anita Roddick sees no reason to seek a softer option after 20 turbulent years selling "green" cosmetics.

"Who wants to lead a quiet life? I'd rather wear out than rust out," she said in an interview at the south-coast base of Body Shop International Plc, the manufacturing and retailing group which she founded in 1976.
Professing not to understand leisure, she maintains: "Life is about work and love and end of story."
Body Shop, run from a building styled like an Asian temple with curved green roofs, now has more than 1,400 mainly franchised stores in 46 countries. South Africa and South Korea come next.
Exotic smells from cosmetics and toiletries like tangerine beer shampoo and marmalade body scrub pervade the offices and the contrasting, very functional grey/green factory buildings.
Roddick, a 53-year-old grandmother who favours slogans like "business as unusual" and "retailing with attitude", prefers to call her group multi-local, not multinational.
Indeed, she would dearly like to change the world economic system and break the power of transnational corporations.

Campaigning for causes ranging from fair trade and saving the rainforests to countering domestic violence is part of a normal day's work at Body Shop. It took a swipe at oil giant Shell when coordinating an international protest at the sentencing and execution of Ogoni environmentalists in Nigeria.

"The Quakers did it. The cooperative movement did it. They were campaigning for social change one way or another," Roddick says, seeing her activism, rooted in the 1960s, as part of a longer tradition.
Words tumble out as the ex-teacher speaks and sentences are often left unfinished as she rushes on.

"We were undeniably counter-culture and we did it our way. And our way was that you bring these issues into the workplace. Business is not about profit. Business is not about private greed. Business is about public good," she insists.
Business schools use the unconventional Body Shop experience as a case study, while Roddick is herself promoting alternative study courses on socially responsible business.

Body Shop has attracted a lot of bad publicity which said it was not as green as it claimed -- particularly on its strong opposition to animal testing, which is emblazoned all over its headquarters and stamped on all its products.
It has denied the claims and is seeking six million names on a petition to back a Europe-wide ban on animal testing.

Almost all ingredients have been tested at some time but it tries to ensure suppliers do not carry out such tests. "We've had to pull products off when we've found that they were tested. I don't know one company that does that," Roddick says.

Her own staff would, she adds, be the first to take action if there were any duplicity. "They'd be out of this company like a bat out of hell if they thought there were any shenanigans going on...because they're activists."
Roddick says many attacks, including an Internet campaign, stem from one journalist acting like a "corporate stalker".

She complains about what she calls the share analysts' "absolute obsession with looking at America as a constant barometer of whether this company will survive" although it is doing well elsewhere, particularly in Asia.
The group's performance in the tough U.S. market, where it lost money last year, was like "two steps forward, one step back. But it's getting better," she added.
Earlier this year Roddick and her husband, Gordon, the group's chairman, shelved plans to buy back the entire share capital of the company, of which they now own around a quarter.
They eventually preferred the now familiar scrutiny under share analysts' microscopes to the risks of being dependent on the banks who would have lent the money.
Asked if a buyback was gone forever, she replied: "You only get one little light and that's when the share price was so low. Now it's gone back up and it'll probably go up and up and up.

"We have to show, certainly to the investors and to the City analysts, new forms of distribution. We have to show the complete new design of the stores which are all coming out this year and some of the old product rationalisation," she adds.

Sales on the Internet may help. The group also hopes its successful Body Shop Direct experiment -- selling at parties in people's homes -- will be a big hit in Latin America and Southeast Asia, fitting in with the local culture.
In some countries it might not have a network of stores, just one or two as a symbol and the rest direct marketing.
A report which the group itself commissioned said it was not good at handling criticism but Roddick attacks media cynicism and calls for the press to show social responsibility.
She takes note of people she respects but says much sniping follows "our inability to just keep quiet and be a cosmetic diva. I haven't got the time for people who just want a crummy story."
Now concentrating on design, development and what the group calls "values and vision", she steers clear of financial detail.

But her frustration to get things done quickly can bring friction. "You end up being more guerrilla within your own company so you can be heard because we (entrepreneurs) have "hurry sickness" that normal managers and operators don't have."
Her ingrained activism is not, however, pulling her towards mainstream party politics. "I think it's more fun for me being a gadfly, nipping at the ankles of the institutions," she says with a smile.
